bibliography.note: Crossref: Savino, Jacqueline F.; Stein, Roy A. 1982 (May). Predator-Prey Interaction between Largemouth Bass and Bluegills as Influenced by Simulated, Submersed Vegetation. Transactions of the American Fisheries Society 111(3): 255-266. Matches the reference entry. Title page not seen

claims.claim: largemouth bass caught bluegill as easily at 50 stems m⁻² as in open water but almost never at 250 or 1,000
claims.note: full text not obtained; a search-engine summary of the abstract says much the same, which confirms nothing

claims.claim: largemouth 33–37 cm on bluegill 35–44 mm: captures per strike ≈ 0.83 without stems, 0.58–0.67 among stems; pools, 16–24 °C
claims.note: the predator and prey sizes, the temperatures and the per-strike successes all need the paper's methods and its table or figure

claims.claim: vegetation reduces encounters and the decision to attack, not success per attack: largemouth attacked bluegill about 31, 26, 3 and almost 0 times an hour at 0, 50, 250 and 1,000 rope stems/m², while success per attack stayed between 0.58 and 0.83
claims.note: check the attack rates (per hour? per bass or per pool?), the stem material ('rope') and whether success per attack really held at 250 and 1,000 stems when attacks were near zero (few attacks, so a success ratio there rests on very few events)

claims.claim: cover cuts attacks, counted once (after Savino & Stein 1982): 'vegetation cuts encounters and attacks, not success per attack'
claims.note: rests on the same finding as the §3.7.1 claim

claims.claim: structure cuts the strike's capture success as well as the encounter (Savino & Stein 1982: at high stem densities largemouth caught few bluegill; capture success falls with complexity)
claims.note: this code comment cites the paper for the OPPOSITE of §3.7.1 and fish3.js:144 (which say success per attack is NOT reduced). COVER_CS is 0 in F3 and set to 0 again at fish3.js:808, so the comment describes a switched-off path; once the text is read, one of the two attributions has to go

claims.claim: the size term is renormalized to 1 at the prey/predator length ratio the successes were measured at: 0.12 for a bass on spiny prey (code: 'largemouth 0.57–0.83 on bluegill at 0.12, Savino & Stein')
claims.note: if the Table 3.7-1 sizes hold, 35–44 mm bluegill on 330–370 mm bass gives a ratio of 0.095–0.133 (≈ 0.12 at the midpoints, project arithmetic) — unverified until the sizes are read. The code's 0.57 differs from the paper's 0.58 (Table 3.7-1, §3.7.1)

claims.claim: structure protects only the fish that use it (Savino & Stein 1982; weed_bed_structure.md §4)
a searching predator's capture falls as 1/(1 + (S/S50)³) with S50 ~150 stems/m² (Crowder & Cooper 1982; Savino & Stein 1982)
claims.note: the curve is the project's fit; the paper can at most supply the points (0, 50, 250, 1,000 stems/m²)
